# ROUND TWO — CANON, PNL ATTRIBUTION, VIDEO/X

## 0. Correction that reframes the whole round

**"Kevin Klassen" does not exist. You mean Timothy Klassen.** PhD particle physics (Chicago) → equity derivatives quant under Emanuel Derman at Goldman (2000) → designed the 2003 "new VIX" for Cboe → built Getco's options analytics infrastructure and quant team → founded Vola Dynamics 2016 (Jim Gatheral is an advisor). Verified: [databento.com/blog/quants-worth-following-timothy-klassen](https://databento.com/blog/quants-worth-following-timothy-klassen), [voladynamics.com/team/timothy-klassen/](https://voladynamics.com/team/timothy-klassen/).

He is simultaneously the single best free source for **(B)** and the main find for **(C)**. Everything below in Section B.1 and C.1 is him. I opened and read the actual PDFs rather than trusting metadata.

---

# (A) THE BOOK CANON, RANKED FOR YOUR POSITION

Ranking premise: you have the surface maths (SVI/SSVI implemented). What you lack is (i) how a book behaves over time, (ii) what the costs actually are, (iii) how to tell whether a model is broken. Books are ranked by marginal value **given that**, not by general quality.

### Access reality first — stated honestly

I could not verify IIT Kharagpur's specific holdings; [library.iitkgp.ac.in](https://library.iitkgp.ac.in/) requires institutional login and its e-resource list is not publicly enumerable. What I can state:

- **ONOS (One Nation One Subscription)**, live Jan 2025 and the thing IIT KGP's library now leads with, is a **journals** deal. It does not cover monographs. Do not expect it to deliver any book on this list.
- Indian institutional subscriptions typically include **Wiley journals**, not **Wiley Online Books**. Sinclair, Taleb, Gatheral, Lopez de Prado and Rebonato are all Wiley — so the most likely outcome is that **none of the Wiley titles are reachable** and you buy them.
- **Springer/Palgrave eBooks** are commonly held by IITs. That makes Leoni (Palgrave) the one title most likely free to you.
- **Cambridge Core** books (Bouchaud) are plausible but institution-specific.
- Natenberg is McGraw-Hill Professional — effectively never in an Indian academic package.

Action: ask the library for the **e-books A–Z list** and specifically whether Wiley Online Books and Cambridge Core Books (not just journals) are in the subscription. That is a two-minute email that resolves ~₹40,000 of purchasing decisions.

---

### Tier 1 — buy these, in this order

**1. Euan Sinclair, *Volatility Trading* (2nd ed., Wiley 2013)**
- **Uniquely gives:** the only book that treats an options trade as a *statistical bet with a cost structure* rather than a payoff diagram. The hedging chapter derives the path-dependence of a delta-hedged option's P&L explicitly — i.e. why your realised P&L is not (σ_realised² − σ_implied²) × vega but a gamma-weighted path integral. The money-management chapter (Kelly, fractional Kelly, drawdown) is where most quant-trained people are actually weakest.
- **Chapters that matter:** volatility measurement/estimators; hedging; money management; trade evaluation. **Skippable:** the introductory BSM derivation, the options-basics chapter.
- **Where dated/wrong:** pre-0DTE, pre-electronic-retail, US-centric. Its vol-forecasting chapter (GARCH-family) is the weakest part and has been overtaken. Nothing on the modern dealer-flow literature.
- **Free equivalent:** none. This is the book with no substitute.
- **Tests:** (2) costs and fills discussed explicitly, (3) 25+ years trading vol, (4) repeatedly names where his own methods fail — **counts double**. Passes cleanly.
- **Caveat:** Sinclair teaches on QuantInsti's paid EPAT programme ([quantinsti.com/faculty/euan-sinclair](https://www.quantinsti.com/faculty/euan-sinclair)). The book does not funnel; his ancillary presence does. Judge the book alone.

**2. Lorenzo Bergomi, *Stochastic Volatility Modeling* (CRC 2016)** — **and Chapters 1 and 2 are free**
- URL: [lorenzobergomi.com/contents-sample-chapters](https://www.lorenzobergomi.com/contents-sample-chapters) — Ch.1 and Ch.2 are direct PDF downloads.
- **Uniquely gives:** the correct answer to "what happens to my book when spot moves." Chapter 1 (24 pp, free, I read it) is titled §1.1 *Characterizing a usable model — the Black-Scholes equation* and §1.2 ***How (in)effective is delta hedging?*** with §1.2.2 *The real case*. It derives the P&L of a delta-hedged short option from break-even accounting, then shows empirically how much hedging error survives. That is Section B's core content, free, from a Société Générale head of quant research.
- **Chapters that matter for you:** 1, 2 (free), 8 (*The smile of stochastic volatility models* — where the skew-stickiness ratio is derived), 9 (*Linking static and dynamic properties*), 10 (*What causes equity smiles?*). **Skippable:** 11 (multi-asset), 12 (LSV) unless you go exotic.
- **Where dated:** written before the 0DTE regime and before rough vol became mainstream; Ch.6 (Heston) is there mostly to be criticised.
- **Free equivalent:** the two free chapters plus his SSRN/paper page [lorenzobergomi.com/papers](https://www.lorenzobergomi.com/papers) (*Smile Dynamics* I–IV) cover perhaps 40% of the book's practical value at zero cost. Read those before deciding to buy.
- **Tests:** (3) built and ran SG's equity-derivatives models, (4) explicitly enumerates where each model class fails and why — double. (5) reproducible.
- **Caveat:** notation is dense and idiosyncratic; there is no code. You will be re-deriving.

**3. Nassim Taleb, *Dynamic Hedging* (Wiley 1997)**
- **Uniquely gives:** the *bookkeeping* of an options book — how a market maker organises risk when he has 500 positions in one name. The vega/volatility-surface chapter and the "bucketing and topography" material are the only book-length treatment of **vega bucketing** written by someone who did it on a desk. Also the only serious treatment of what happens between the greeks (the "delta paradox", pin risk, wing risk, dividend/early-exercise pathologies).
- **Chapters that matter:** the greek "modules" section; vega and the volatility surface; bucketing/topography; the American-options and pin-risk chapters. **Skippable:** the philosophical asides, the exotic-pricing chapters (superseded), anything on rates.
- **Where dated or wrong:** pre-smile-model. It predates SVI, SABR, everything you have implemented. It has no coherent spot-vol dynamics — precisely the gap Bergomi and Klassen fill. Its exotics pricing is obsolete. Read it *for the taxonomy of risk*, not for models.
- **Free equivalent:** none, and nothing has replaced it.
- **Tests:** (3) traded, (4) the entire book is a catalogue of where textbook greeks stop working — double. Passes.
- **Caveat:** badly organised, badly edited, and Taleb's later public persona has made people dismiss the book. Do not. But budget for frustration.

**4. Bouchaud, Bonart, Donier, Gould, *Trades, Quotes and Prices* (CUP 2018)**
- **Uniquely gives:** the cost side, quantitatively. Square-root impact law, order-flow long memory, the propagator model, why your backtest's fill assumptions are the dominant error term. This is the discipline that makes "pure research usable in a trade."
- **Chapters that matter:** the impact chapters (square-root law, propagators), order-book statistics, and the market-making/liquidity chapters. **Skippable:** the latent-liquidity theory chapters unless you go deep.
- **Where dated:** equities/futures-centric; options microstructure is essentially absent, which matters because NIFTY option books behave differently from the underlying.
- **Free equivalent — real one:** Bouchaud, Farmer & Lillo, *How Markets Slowly Digest Changes in Supply and Demand*, [arXiv:0809.0822](https://arxiv.org/abs/0809.0822). ~100 pages, free, covers a large fraction of Parts II–III. **Read this before buying the book.**
- **Tests:** (3) Bouchaud runs CFM, (4) explicit about the domain of validity of the square-root law, (5) reproducible on minute data — you have it. Passes.
- **Caveat:** it will not tell you anything specific about Indian markets, and impact calibration on NIFTY options is unpublished territory.

---

### Tier 2 — worth owning, conditionally

**5. Euan Sinclair, *Positional Option Trading* (Wiley 2020).** The value is the negative result: he argues most named option "strategies" carry no edge and that the edge, where it exists, is in position sizing, selection and exit. Chapters on bet sizing and on the psychology/process are the keepers. Skippable: the strategy-by-strategy catalogue. Caveat: substantial overlap with *Volatility Trading*; buy second, not first.

**6. Sheldon Natenberg, *Option Volatility and Pricing* (2nd ed. 2015).** For you, ~70% is below your level. The parts that are not: the "risk considerations" material on how a spread's greeks migrate as spot and time move, and the market-maker chapters added in the 2nd edition. **Free equivalent:** Harel Jacobson's *Think Like a Market Maker* covers the useful residue ([volquant.medium.com/think-like-a-market-maker-understanding-implied-volatility-b53c25739aa0](https://volquant.medium.com/think-like-a-market-maker-understanding-implied-volatility-b53c25739aa0)). **Recommendation: skip the purchase.** Fails test (2) — no cost model anywhere.

**7. Jim Gatheral, *The Volatility Surface* (Wiley 2006).** You have already absorbed the parametrisation content via SVI/SSVI. What remains valuable: the *dynamics of the volatility skew* chapter and the variance-swap/vol-derivatives chapter. **Free equivalent:** his Baruch MFE lecture notes and slides, [mfe.baruch.cuny.edu](https://mfe.baruch.cuny.edu/) — these overlap the book heavily and are free. **Recommendation: use the notes, skip the book.**

**8. Peter Leoni, *The Greeks and Hedging Explained* (Palgrave 2014).** Short, cheap, and the publisher's own description names exactly your Section-B gaps: *"themes omitted from textbooks but which occur in practice — including the effect of day conventions, interest rates and sticky deltas."* Author: PhD math physics, KBC Asset Management risk, ING exotics front-office quant, then GDF Suez / Macquarie trading. [link.springer.com/book/10.1057/9781137350749](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1057/9781137350749). **Most likely title on this list to be free via your institution** (Springer/Palgrave). Caveat: thin — it is a monograph, not a reference; it will not replace Bergomi.

**9. Marcos Lopez de Prado, *Advances in Financial Machine Learning* (Wiley 2018).** Include it *only* for four things: the triple-barrier labelling scheme, meta-labelling, purged/embargoed cross-validation, and the deflated Sharpe ratio. Those four are genuinely load-bearing if you ever run an ML overlay on option signals. Everything else — HRP, fractional differentiation, the structural-break chapters — is contested and I found no independent practitioner reproduction that vindicates them. **Free equivalent:** Chapter 1 is free on SSRN ([abstract 3104847](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3104847)) and his code sits at quantresearch.org. **Honest negative:** I searched specifically for a substantive published critique of AFML's reproducibility and did not find one from a credible named practitioner — the criticism circulates as forum folklore, not as a citable document. Treat the book's claims as unvalidated rather than validated.

---

### Tier 3 — do not buy

**10. Riccardo Rebonato, *Volatility and Correlation* (2nd ed. 2004).** Parts III and IV — the majority of the book — are interest-rate volatility (LMM, CEV rates, Markov-chain rates). Irrelevant to NIFTY index options. Parts I–II are good but wholly superseded by Bergomi for your purposes. **Skip.**

**11. Euan Sinclair, *Option Trading* (2010).** Largely superseded by his other two. Its market-making-techniques chapter (Ch.10) is the one distinctive piece.

**12. Mack & Sinclair, *Retail Options Trading* (2024, self-published, ~377 pp).** Verified to exist. Positioned at retail-scale edge-finding with Kelly sizing. Reviews are split on level — one credible review says it oscillates between explaining what a long call is and computing rolling VIX z-scores. Given your level, **skip**.

**Books that arguably earn a slot and were not on your list:** Derman & Miller, *The Volatility Smile* (2016) — but Derman's Columbia lecture notes are free and cover most of it. Larry Harris, *Trading and Exchanges* (2002) — the canonical market-structure text, still unmatched, and cheap. Lehalle & Laruelle, *Market Microstructure in Practice* — execution-cost companion to Bouchaud.

---

# (B) PNL ATTRIBUTION AND GREEK BOOKKEEPING

**Headline finding: the field is real, it is documented, and almost all of the good free material was published in the last 18 months by one person — Timothy Klassen. Round one missed it because it searched for "PnL attribution" as an academic topic rather than as a vendor/desk engineering problem.**

### B.1 — Vola Dynamics: the primary corpus

All free, no registration, named author with the CV above. Index page: **[voladynamics.com/media/](https://voladynamics.com/media/)**

**(a) *Spot-vol Dynamics and Deltas for SPX Options*, subtitled "Does anyone know how to calculate the correct delta of a vanilla option?"**
[voladynamics.com/pdf/Vola_SpotVolDynamicsDeltasSPX_LI_20200107.pdf](https://voladynamics.com/pdf/Vola_SpotVolDynamicsDeltasSPX_LI_20200107.pdf) (13 pp — I read all of it)

**What it concretely gives you, and it is directly executable on your minute data:**
- The exact statement δ = δ_BS + vega · (∂σ/∂F), so the whole delta problem reduces to estimating dVdF.
- The estimation recipe: *"the (realized) vol sensitivities can be determined reasonably well using, say, one day's worth of 1-minute or 5-minute snapshot data using a linear regression, with some outlier treatment for robustness."* You are about to receive minute-wise NIFTY data. This is a one-day project.
- The independent check: regress vol changes on forward changes **per strike** to get an empirical dVdF curve, then compare against the one-snapshot model prediction. He shows the two agree.
- Concrete numbers: SSR ≈ 1.3 typical, → 2.0 on big down days, 1 ≤ SSR ≤ 2 with theoretical reason, **KOSPI often above 2** (the one named non-US index — relevant, since NIFTY may behave more like KOSPI than SPX).
- Magnitude of the error you are currently making: ATM delta adjustment ≈ −0.06; put-wing peak ≈ −0.08; and **in the call wing above NS ≈ 1.2 the correct delta is essentially zero while naive BS delta is still 0.03** — a 100% relative error on tradable OTM calls.
- Explicit falsification: *"the 'null-hypothesis' … namely 'sticky-strike', would mean that dVdF is flat at 0. The above results reject that idea on both the absolute and standard deviation level conclusively (ditto for 'sticky-delta' dynamics, or any simple 'combination' of the two)."*
- And the subtlety most people get wrong: **SSR = 1 does not mean sticky-strike.** It means sticky-strike *at the money only*; the wings still move. He shows a day (2018-01-22) where SSR ≈ 1 and dVdF is strongly non-zero in both wings.
- **Tests passed:** (2) — the whole point is quote/spread-aware fitting and he discusses wide markets and error bars; (3) — Getco, Goldman, Cboe; (4) — names where the linear-dVdF approximation "breaks down so dramatically for NS > 0.5", and gives the proof (negative ATF curvature means the ATM parabola cannot describe the call-wing knee); (5) — reproducible on any minute-level option chain, including yours. **Four of five, with (4) double.**
- **Honest caveat:** this is marketing collateral for a paid C++ library. The self-serving claim is explicit — *"Good vol curves that can actually match the market implied vols for liquid names (none in the public domain do)"*. Since you built SVI, take that as a hypothesis to test, not a fact.

**(b) *Real-Time Implied Volatility Surfaces: A Practitioner's View of the Black Arts*, Cboe RMC Quant Conference, 2 Oct 2025** (100 slides)
[voladynamics.com/pdf/Klassen_IVS-BlackArts_CBOE_20251002_distrib.pdf](https://voladynamics.com/pdf/Klassen_IVS-BlackArts_CBOE_20251002_distrib.pdf)

Read slide 74, "**Spot-Vol Dynamics Myths**", which is your Section-B question answered in eight lines:
> *Myth: common "vol regimes" are "sticky-by-strike" or "sticky-by-delta". **Sticky-strike scenarios are still commonly used by risk departments.** In equities, at least, neither has happened for 20y+. Sticky-delta implies SSR=0 for all terms. Never happens. Sticky-strike implies SSR=1 (i.e. sticky-strike around ATM). Even when vols are sticky-by-strike around ATM, they never are in the wings.*

Also in this deck and directly relevant to you:
- Slide 6 and 58: **a quantitative attack on the model you already implemented.** SVI/S5 has "not much shape flexibility, e.g. they do not allow W-shapes as required around events." Of ~5,630 OPRA names, only ~1.2% are bias-free-fittable with SVI; SSVI manages 73%; **SPX/SPY/ES need 16–18 parameters and some market makers use ~25**. Empirical scaling: nParams ≈ (nOptions/5)^(1/3). On IBIT he shows fits "13–70× better than SVI" in the price-difference metric, which he calls "the ultimate test."
- Slide 68: SSR has *term structure* now, can exceed 2 or fall below 1 at the short end, and shows horizon dependence (1-min vs 5-min vs intraday-vs-overnight). If you estimate SSR from 1-minute NIFTY data you will get a different number than from close-to-close, and he says so.
- Slides 82–99: the "vol time" (business/trading time) machinery, event times, and **settlement effects including exchange and bank holidays** — the exact mechanism behind your weekend/holiday theta question.
- **Caveat:** slides without narration. Many pages are plots with two-line captions. You will get maybe 60% of the value without the talk audio.

**(c) The 2025 video series** — short, free, named, no funnel. Verified titles via YouTube oEmbed:
| Video | URL | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **PnL Attribution #1: The Greeks** | [youtube.com/watch?v=GM2vWXKtx6U](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GM2vWXKtx6U) | The Taylor/greek decomposition on a real book |
| **PnL Attribution #2: Scenarios** | [youtube.com/watch?v=VNhMExVMlpc](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VNhMExVMlpc) | Full-revaluation attribution vs greek attribution — i.e. where the unexplained residual comes from |
| **Thetas and Time Conventions** | [youtube.com/watch?v=35l1FoQ9RvY](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=35l1FoQ9RvY) | Calendar-day vs trading-day theta, exactly your question |
| **Sticky-by-Strike or Sticky-by-Delta? Neither!** | [youtube.com/watch?v=ShluExtp5xA](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ShluExtp5xA) | |
| **If sticky strike is not the answer, what is?** | [youtube.com/watch?v=jDTC2hqFTCU](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jDTC2hqFTCU) | Calibrating SSR |
| **Event Modeling: Decomposing Vol Surfaces Around Events** | [youtube.com/watch?v=7Ni8ihAs6vA](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7Ni8ihAs6vA) | Two-jump Merton event model; RBI policy / budget / election analogue for NIFTY |

There is a matching LinkedIn article, *Thetas and Time Conventions in the Vola Library* (Dec 2025), listed on the media page. **I could not open LinkedIn** (login wall) — flagging that rather than paraphrasing a summary of it.

### B.2 — Bergomi Chapter 1, free — the derivation itself

[lorenzobergomi.com/contents-sample-chapters](https://www.lorenzobergomi.com/contents-sample-chapters) → Chapter 1 PDF (24 pp).

Gives you the P&L decomposition from first principles as an *accounting identity*, not a model result — his framing: *"a pricing equation is essentially an analytical accounting device: rather than predicting anything about the future dynamics of the underlying securities, a model's pricing equation supplies a decomposition of the profit and loss (P&L) experienced on a derivative position as time elapses."* Then §1.2 *How (in)effective is delta hedging?* with §1.2.2 *The real case* quantifies the residual. **Tests:** (3), (4) — double, (5). **Caveat:** no code, and it stops before multi-factor vega attribution, which is Chapters 8–9 (paid).

### B.3 — The regulator has already answered "how much unexplained P&L means the model is broken"

**BCBS d457, *Minimum capital requirements for market risk* (Jan 2019).** Primary PDF: **[bis.org/bcbs/publ/d457.pdf](https://www.bis.org/bcbs/publ/d457.pdf)** — I downloaded and read the relevant chapters.

**MAR32 — the P&L Attribution (PLA) test.** This is the only quantitative, published, universally-applied standard for "is my risk model explaining my P&L." Exact content:
- Compare **RTPL** (risk-model valuation P&L) against **HPL** (hypothetical P&L: yesterday's positions revalued with today's market data, no intraday trading, no new deals, fees and commissions excluded) — MAR32.20, 32.25, 32.26.
- Two metrics on a **rolling 250-day** window (MAR32.34–32.41): **Spearman rank correlation** of the two P&L series, and the **Kolmogorov–Smirnov** statistic (max absolute gap between the two empirical CDFs).
- **Thresholds (MAR32.42), verbatim:** green requires correlation **> 0.80 AND KS < 0.09** (p = 0.264). Red is correlation **< 0.70 OR KS > 0.12** (p = 0.055). Anything between is amber and carries a capital surcharge.
- Note MAR32.27 footnote 2, which is precisely your theta question: *"P&L due to the passage of time should be included in the APL and should be treated consistently in both HPL and RTPL. Time effects can include… the theta effect… and carry or costs of funding."* The regulator's answer to calendar-vs-business time is **"pick one and be consistent across all three P&L measures"** — inconsistency there is itself a model failure.

**MAR21 — the published vega bucketing specification.** Equity vega risk factors are defined *along one dimension only, the maturity of the option*, mapped to tenors **0.5, 1, 3, 5, 10 years** (MAR21.8–21.14). Within-bucket vega correlation is ρ = min(ρ_delta × ρ_maturity, 1) with ρ_maturity = exp(−α|T_k − T_l| / min(T_k,T_l)) and **α = 1%** (MAR21.93, 21.95).

**The instructive negative:** the Basel standard **does not bucket equity vega by strike or moneyness at all**. Skew risk is pushed into the curvature charge and the residual-risk add-on. So the regulator's own bucketing scheme is deliberately cruder than what your book needs. Use MAR21 as the *floor* — a strike-bucketed vega grid is a strict improvement, and the α = 1% maturity-decay kernel is a defensible, free, published starting point for your own correlation matrix.

- **Tests:** (2) — the whole standard is about valuation and cost adjustments; (3) — written by the people who supervise real books; (4) — MAR32.45 explicitly discusses when the test itself fails ("regime shift", "cross-border financial market stress") — double; (5) — fully reproducible, it is arithmetic.
- **Honest caveat, and it is a real one:** the PLA test compares **model P&L to model P&L** (RTPL vs HPL), *not* model P&L to realised cash. It answers "is my risk system consistent with my pricing system," which is a weaker question than "is my model right about the market." It is also distributional over 250 days, so it gives you **no per-day threshold** for "today's residual is too big." For that, you have to set your own bar — and nobody has published one.

### B.4 — Managing Smile Risk: the primary document on reported delta being wrong

**Hagan, Kumar, Lesniewski, Woodward, *Managing Smile Risk*, Wilmott, 2002.** Free PDF: [deriscope.com/docs/Hagan_2002.pdf](https://www.deriscope.com/docs/Hagan_2002.pdf).

Everyone cites this as "the SABR paper." Its actual thesis is your Section-B question: local-volatility models predict that when spot falls the smile shifts to *higher* prices, whereas real smiles move *with* the underlying — so "delta and vega hedges derived from the model can be unstable and may perform worse than naive Black-Scholes hedges." The backbone concept (how ATM vol moves as the forward moves) is the rates-market ancestor of Bergomi's SSR and Klassen's dVdF. **Tests:** (3) — Hagan/Lesniewski were at Bear Stearns/BNP; (4) — the paper's central claim *is* a failure-mode statement about the then-dominant model, double; (5). **Caveat:** rates/swaptions-native. The SABR parametrisation itself is inferior to what you already have; read it for the diagnosis, not the cure.

### B.5 — Ahmad & Wilmott, *Which Free Lunch Would You Like Today, Sir?*

Wilmott magazine, 2005. Landing page: [wilmott.com/which-free-lunch-would-you-like-today-sir-delta-hedging-volatility-arbitrage-and-optimal-portfolios-riaz-ahmad-and-paul-wilmott/](https://www.wilmott.com/which-free-lunch-would-you-like-today-sir-delta-hedging-volatility-arbitrage-and-optimal-portfolios-riaz-ahmad-and-paul-wilmott/).

Closed-form expected P&L **and variance of P&L** for hedging at three distinct volatilities — true, implied, and your own hedge vol — for a single option and for a portfolio. This is the analytic result behind the empirical fact that "I was right about vol and still lost money." **Tests:** (4) — it is entirely about the dispersion of outcomes when you are right on average; (5) — trivially reproducible. **Caveat:** I could not find a clean free PDF on a stable primary host; the free copies I located are on Scribd/ResearchGate. Fails a strict primary-source standard. Your institutional access likely reaches it via Wilmott's archive.

### B.6 — Honest negatives on (B)

- **There is no credible open-source P&L-explain engine.** I searched GitHub systematically. The best-known hit, [github.com/philippchan/optionsPnL](https://github.com/philippchan/optionsPnL), is a **single Jupyter notebook** (delta/gamma/theta/vega/volga/vanna decomposition with a residual, plus plots). Everything else returned by a targeted GitHub search is a **zero-star toy repo**. Every production implementation is commercial and closed (Vola Dynamics, Murex, Bloomberg MARS). **Conclusion: you will write this yourself, and that is a genuine, defensible piece of work.**
- **The Wikipedia article "PnL explained" is the only free general reference**, and it is thin. That is a statement about the field, not about Wikipedia.
- **Burghardt & Hanweck, "Calendar-Adjusted Volatilities," *Journal of Derivatives*, Winter 1993** is the seminal citation for business-time vs calendar-time variance weighting. I could not reach a free copy, and Portfolio Management Research (which owns JOD) is rarely in Indian institutional packages. Flagging this as **unreachable rather than substituting a blog summary of it**.
- Round one's Moontower has two directly on-topic free posts (weekend theta; cleaning implied vols). Already covered — not re-reported, but do not skip them because of that.

### B.7 — The Indian weekend/holiday problem: the two primary documents

You need these because the business-time question in India is now a *moving target*, not a constant.

1. **NSE Circular 103/2025, Download Ref NSE/FAOP/68589, 17 June 2025 — "Revision in Expiry Day of Index and Stock derivatives contracts."** Primary PDF, verified: [nsearchives.nseindia.com/content/circulars/FAOP68589.pdf](https://nsearchives.nseindia.com/content/circulars/FAOP68589.pdf). Contracts expiring on or before 31 Aug 2025 keep Thursday; contracts expiring on or after **1 Sep 2025 expire Tuesday**, with monthlies on the **last Tuesday**. It cites its parent: **SEBI/HO/MRD/TPD-1/P/CIR/2025/76 dated 26 May 2025**, *Final Settlement Day (Expiry Day) for Equity Derivatives Contracts*.
2. **The NSE trading-holiday circular for the relevant year** (same `nsearchives.nseindia.com/content/circulars/` path). India runs ~14–16 exchange holidays, unevenly clustered around Oct–Nov. That is the driver: a Tuesday-expiry weekly spans 7 calendar days but between **3 and 5 trading days** depending on the week. A calendar-day theta will mis-state a Diwali-week weekly by a large fraction, and the mis-statement flips sign across the holiday.

Why this matters more than in the US: with a Tuesday expiry, the *weekend now sits in the middle of the option's life*, not at the start. Under a calendar-day convention your Monday theta and your Friday theta are the same number; under trading-day they are not, and the difference is the entire P&L of a short weekly on a holiday week. **Nobody has published on business-time theta calibration for NIFTY weeklies.** That is a real gap, and with minute data you are positioned to close it: estimate intraday vs overnight vs weekend variance shares directly from 1-minute returns, then compare the implied vol you back out under each time convention.

---

# (C) THE VIDEO AND X LAYER

### Deribit API reference (`docs.deribit.com`) + live JSON-RPC
**https://docs.deribit.com/** · **https://www.deribit.com/api/v2/public/get_instruments?currency=BTC&kind=option**

Tests passed: (1) runnable, (5) reproducible. Caveat: the docs index page is nearly contentless — go to `docs.deribit.com/llms.txt` for the real page list, or skip docs and introspect the live API, which is what I did.

### Contract Introduction Policy — the published expiry and strike ladder
**https://support.deribit.com/hc/en-us/articles/25944688876957-Contract-Introduction-Policy**

The exchange's own listing rules. BTC options: 4 dailies, 3 weeklies, 3 monthlies, 4 quarterlies. Strike intervals by bracket:

| TTE | ATM | Outer | Wings |
|---|---|---|---|
| ≤ 4 days | $500 | $500 | $1,000 |
| 1 week / 1 month | $1,000 | $2,000 | $5,000 |
| 3 months | $2,000 | $5,000 | $10,000 |

ETH: $20/$50/$100 → $100/$200/$500. Strikes are listed to cover **0.1–0.9 delta**, and "ATM" means 40–60 delta, "wings" <20 delta.

My measured ladder confirms it exactly — 29AUG26 shows spacings `{500: 14, 1000: 12}`, 25SEP26 shows `{1000: 20, 5000: 19, 2000: 16, 20000: 6}`. **This is the single biggest structural difference from NIFTY**: Deribit strike spacing is a step function of tenor and moneyness, not a constant. Your surface fitter cannot assume a uniform grid, and the far expiries carry strikes to $320,000 against a $79k spot — a 4× call. NIFTY gives you a dense uniform ladder over a narrow band; Deribit gives you a sparse non-uniform ladder over an enormous band.

Also buried here and materially new: *"when an option expires in the money, it is first physically settled into the corresponding futures contract at the strike price, which then cash settles… live for all linear options from early April 2026."*

Tests passed: (5), and (4) in the weak sense that it states its own discretion to deviate. Caveat: it explicitly says the tables are "a guide only" and Deribit may alter intervals; treat the API as truth, the policy as intent.

### Index Prices + Settlement (the 30-minute TWAP)
**https://support.deribit.com/hc/en-us/articles/25944739377309-Index-Prices** · **https://support.deribit.com/hc/en-us/articles/29734325712413-Settlement**

Index is a **capped-median**, not a plain median: each constituent is clamped to ±0.5% of the initial median, then a weighted average of the clamped values is taken. Circuit breaker halts derivatives if the index moves >10% between 1-second ticks; a constituent that fails to update for 3 minutes is dropped; with only two sources live the max allowed spread is 2.5%. BTC/USD and ETH/USD "typically have five or more constituents."

Settlement: delivery price = **30-minute TWAP of the index, 07:30–08:00 UTC, sampled every 4 seconds** (450 samples). Options are European, cash-settled, auto-exercised.

The part that actually changes behaviour: **delta of expiring options decays linearly to zero over the last 30 minutes**, and the risk matrix underlying converges to the Estimated Delivery Price, so *"a -10% scenario 15 min into expiry will actually use the underlying value if the index were to move -5%."* If you pin-risk trade, your reported delta from the API goes to ~0 on a deep ITM call near 08:00. That is a deliberate exchange convention, not a bug, and it will silently break a naive hedger.

Tests passed: (5), (4) — the index article enumerates its own manipulation attack surface and the mitigations. Caveat: the page opens with *"These are for educational purposes only, the below are not official Deribit policies."* The exchange is disclaiming its own methodology document, which is worth knowing before you build settlement logic on it.

### Fees — and the fee cap that dominates short-dated crypto options
**https://support.deribit.com/hc/en-us/articles/25944746248989-Fees**

Standard tier options: **3 bps of underlying notional, capped at 12.5% of premium**, maker = taker. Block 3 bps. Option combos with at least one buy and one sell leg get the cheaper direction's fees zeroed — straddles and strangles do **not** qualify (all legs same direction).

I worked the cap through at spot $79,398:

| Premium | as % spot | Fee (one way) | % of premium | Round trip | Binding |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $100 | 0.13% | $12.50 | 12.50% | **25.0%** | cap |
| $190 | 0.24% | $23.75 | 12.50% | **25.0%** | cap |
| $437 | 0.55% | $23.82 | 5.45% | 10.9% | notional |
| $1,826 | 2.30% | $23.82 | 1.30% | 2.6% | notional |
| $7,275 | 9.16% | $23.82 | 0.33% | 0.7% | notional |

The cap binds below premium = 0.0003/0.125 = **0.24% of spot**. Below that you pay a flat 12.5% each way — 25% round trip. Above it you pay a fixed $23.82 per BTC regardless of the option's value.

**This is the single most important number for a crypto vol trader and it has no NIFTY analogue.** NSE charges on premium; Deribit charges on notional. Every OTM wing and every short-dated option on Deribit carries a fee that is enormous relative to its premium. Any strategy that trades cheap options frequently — gamma scalping the dailies, wing-buying, ratio structures — is dead on arrival at retail fee tier.

Tests passed: (2) explicitly and quantitatively, (5). Caveat: tiers move fast and VIP1 needs $100k USDC equity; assume standard tier.

### My measurement: the tick size is the hidden tax
Deribit's inverse-option tick is a fixed **BTC** amount, so its USD value scales with spot, and the `tick_size_steps` jump at 0.005 BTC means an option priced just above that has a tick of 0.0005 BTC ≈ **$40**.

| Expiry | n (2-sided) | median tick as % of premium | median quoted spread % | median ticks wide | median premium |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 29AUG26 | 41 | 2.41% | **16.87%** | 10.0 | $1,648 |
| 30AUG26 | 48 | 2.80% | **16.58%** | 6.0 | $1,241 |
| 1SEP26 | 54 | 2.86% | 11.46% | 4.0 | $1,092 |
| 4SEP26 | 61 | 2.08% | 6.67% | 4.0 | $1,866 |
| 25SEP26 | 112 | 0.66% | 3.18% | 4.5 | $6,044 |
| 25JUN27 | 100 | 0.33% | 2.06% | 6.0 | $12,148 |

Across all two-sided BTC options with premium < $500 (n=194): **median tick = 9.09% of premium, median quoted spread = 24.00%.**

Your edge must exceed roughly 50% of premium. **Conclusion: the Deribit wings and dailies are untradeable at retail size, and this is a fee-and-tick fact, not a liquidity opinion.** Concentrate on 25SEP26/25DEC26 where OI is 69% of the book and spreads are 2–3%.

Two things an equity-index trader would not predict, both directly observable:

1. **The skew sign flips with tenor.** Short-dated BTC risk reversals are *positive* — calls bid over puts by 1–2.4 vol points — and go negative only beyond ~90 days. ETH is call-skewed essentially the whole curve. In SPX the risk reversal is negative at every tenor and steepens with maturity; here it is positive at the front and mildly negative at the back. Any model you port from equities with a hard-coded negative ρ will fight the front of this surface.
2. **Term structure is in steep contango** (33 → 42.5 for BTC) while the front is call-skewed. That combination — cheap near vol, call-skewed, upward-sloping — is the crypto signature.

Butterflies are uniformly positive and remarkably stable at +0.7 to +1.4 across the whole curve for both coins, which is the one thing that *does* look like equities.

### Echenim, Gobet & Maurice — "Unbiasing and robustifying implied volatility calibration in a cryptocurrency market with large bid-ask spreads and missing quotes" (Kaiko)
**https://marketing.kaiko.com/hubfs/Factsheets/KAIKO_IVSmile_Methodology.pdf**

**This is the single best answer to "does SVI calibrate here, and what broke."** Free full PDF, CNRS/École Polytechnique authors with Kaiko's quant data lead, using real Deribit BTC data.

What it concretely gives you:
- A **theorem** (their Thm 3.1) that calibrating SVI on mid-prices produces a *systematic underestimation* of implied vol in the wings. Not a heuristic — a proof, with the direction of the bias.
- The reason: *"the relative tick size (and thus the relative spread) for options on cryptos is roughly 10 to 50 times larger than for options on traditional markets."* My own measurement above independently confirms this — 9% of premium in the wings.
- An **"anchor price"** built from bid and ask whose bias is third-order in the tick size, replacing the mid.

### Deribit's own inverse-option specification and Black-Scholes convention
**https://support.deribit.com/hc/en-us/articles/31424939096093-Inverse-Options**

Read this before you fit anything. The exchange publishes its exact formulas: `C = X·N(d1) − K·N(d2)·e^(−RT)`, with **X = index**, **F = forward**, and the interest rate *defined* as `R = ln(F/X)/T`. Crucially: *"The implied volatility displayed uses the forward, rather than the index, as the underlying price."* Get this wrong and your IVs will disagree with the screen by a spread-sized amount, and you will spend a week chasing it.

**On the weekend effect** — this article answers it definitively and it is not what folklore says: *"The full amount of time is included in the calculations,"* with the worked example `(1 + 17/24)/365`. Deribit uses **pure calendar time, no business-day or weekend weighting whatsoever.** So the weekend "effect" is not a modelling artefact you must undo — it is a genuine, tradeable dip in quoted IV going into Friday, because the exchange charges the trader for calendar theta the market knows will not be delivered. Whether that dip is *exploitable* net of the 25%-of-premium round-trip on short-dated options in §1 is precisely the question, and I found nobody who has published the answer with costs.

Also here: **options are limit-order-only — market orders are not accepted by the matching engine.** And the allowed trading bandwidth is derived from the portfolio-margin risk matrix plus a constant of 0.015, with orders outside it silently adjusted rather than rejected.

Tests passed: (5), (2) — mistrade rules, adjustment windows and the 2-hour claim deadline are all stated. Caveat: it is exchange documentation, so it describes intent; the mistrade section makes clear that "theoretical price" is ultimately settled by consulting primary market makers, which is a discretionary backstop you cannot model.

I could **not** find a credible, cost-aware empirical study of the BTC/ETH surface around scheduled events — ETF decisions, halvings, CPI/FOMC. ## 3. DVOL

### Methodology
**https://insights.deribit.com/exchange-updates/dvol-deribit-implied-volatility-index/**

Full construction, and it differs from VIX in ways that matter:
- Picks the two expiries bracketing 30 days, **ignoring any instrument listed less than 1 hour ago** (so spreads can normalise).
- Price per instrument is a **depth-VWAP**, not a mid: walk 5 levels or 2 BTC cumulative, take `(DepthAsk + DepthBid)/2`. Fallback chain if the spread is too wide: last-minute trade VWAP → mark price from 60–90s ago.
- **Discards ITM options and anything under 5 delta** — explicitly to avoid strikes where tick size swamps vega, which is the same pathology I measured in §1.
- Forward from the call/put synthetic; strike cutoff at the strike nearest forward.
- Variance-swap integral, interpolate the two expiries, then **EMA over the last 240 one-second points**.

**What it does not measure:** it is not a pure 30-day variance swap rate. The 5-delta truncation means it systematically **understates** the true variance swap strike (it throws away the tails that a variance swap pays on) — the same direction of error as the Kaiko mid-price bias, and for a related reason. The 240-point EMA also means DVOL *lags* by construction; it is unsuitable as a realtime signal for anything faster than a few minutes. And the depth-VWAP construction means DVOL moves when *liquidity* changes, not only when vol changes.

Tests passed: (5) — fully reproducible; (4) — it names the delta truncation and the reason for it. Caveat: Deribit calls this a "whitepaper" but there is no separate PDF with proofs; the article is the spec. Several construction details (exact interpolation weights, EMA seeding) are described in prose, not formulas.

### Is it tradeable? Measured answer: **no.**

`get_instruments?currency=USDC` across all kinds returns exactly **one** DVOL instrument: `BTCDVOL_USDC-30SEP26`. Live state:

```
bid 40.0 / ask 41.0        (a full vol point wide, 2.5%)
open_interest    8.1       (~$324 notional)
24h volume       4.0       (= $160)
last trade       one, 2026-08-28T08:36 UTC
```

Book beyond the touch: bids 42 @ 40, 50 @ 39, 49.9 @ 38 …; asks 20.2 @ 41, 25 @ 41.1, then a gap to 45, 50, 55 — and a 1-lot ask at **352**. There is no ETH DVOL future at all (though the ETH DVOL *index* is live and queryable).

The Contract Introduction Policy confirms this is by design: BTC DVOL has **"1 monthly"** listing, rolled a week before the prior one expires. So the entire crypto listed-vol complex is one monthly contract with three-figure daily turnover, three years after launch.

**Conclusion: DVOL is an excellent free measurement instrument and a non-existent trading instrument.** Treat it as a data series, never as a hedge. The SignalPlus piece (https://insights.deribit.com/industry/demystifying-dvol-futures/) explains correctly why replicating it with vanillas is hard — you need the variance replication *plus* a vol-of-vol convexity adjustment — but it was written at launch in 2023 and its optimism about calendar spreads and ETH/BTC DVOL relative value never materialised, because those instruments do not exist.

**The valuable part is the free index history.** `public/get_volatility_index_data` returns OHLC for BTC and ETH DVOL and I verified data returns for March of 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 — a multi-year, free, primary 30-day IV series at arbitrary resolution. That is your VRP measurement input (§4).

## 4. The crypto variance risk premium

### Almeida, Grith, Miftachov & Wang — "Risk Premia in the Bitcoin Market"
**https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.15195** (free, arXiv)

The most rigorous current measurement. Deribit options plus realized returns. Headline numbers:
- **BVRP averages 14% annualized** at the one-month horizon, versus **~2% for the S&P 500** (Bollerslev-Tauchen-Zhou).
- Bitcoin premium averages **66%/yr**; Martin-style lower bound 66%, Chabi-Yo/Loudis bound 84%.
- Sharpe ~0.8, roughly double SPX.
- The regime result is the useful one: clustering option-implied RNDs yields two volatility regimes, and **BVRP is high in the low-vol regime and lower in high-vol states** — i.e. the premium is *not* highest when vol is highest. They read this as investors being most concerned about variance and *upside* risk when things are calm, which fits the positive front-end call skew I measured.
- Return-premium decomposition: **large positive returns (+20% to +60%) account for 39% of the Bitcoin premium**, versus under a third of SPX's premium coming from positive returns at all. The right tail carries the information in crypto. This is the cleanest statement I found of why equity intuition inverts here.

Tests passed: (5) — Deribit data, method fully specified; (4) — the regime conditioning *is* the failure-mode statement, and they are explicit that the point estimate of the first-moment premium is noisy. Caveat: **no transaction costs anywhere in the paper**, and the sample ends before the 2025–26 regime. A 14% variance premium is comfortably inside the round-trip costs of §1 for short-dated options, so this is a statement about the risk-neutral/physical gap, not about a harvestable return. Do not read 14% as a strategy Sharpe.

### Is it still positive in 2026, and where has it decayed?
**I could not verify this from a primary source, and I want to be blunt about it.** Every 2026 claim I found — "BTC IV overstates RV by 10–15 vol points," "the premium has faded" — traces to vendor blogs or exchange-affiliated commentary with no published methodology. The Deribit "contango → VRP mean +15 points" figure circulates widely and I could not find its underlying calculation.

The structural fact I *can* verify is that the venue landscape shifted: Deribit's share of BTC options open interest reportedly fell below 39% in Jan 2026 (from >90% in 2020) after IBIT ETF options launched in Nov 2024. If true, that fragments the flow that historically generated the premium, and any Deribit-only VRP measurement after 2024 is measuring a shrinking slice. I could not confirm the 39% figure from a primary exchange or OCC source.

**What you should do instead of citing anyone:** DVOL history is free back to at least 2022 (§3), and minute-wise BTC spot is trivially obtainable. Compute `DVOL²` versus subsequent 30-day realized variance yourself, split by the Almeida et al. regime definition. That is a two-day project, it is genuinely original for 2026, and it settles the question with your own measurement rather than an assertion. This is the highest-value piece of unclaimed work in the entire brief.

## 5. Perp-vs-option basis and the option-implied funding relation

### My measurement: the triangle is closed

Put-call parity for inverse options is `C − P = (F − K)/F` in coin terms, so `F = K/(1 − (C−P))`. I computed the parity-implied forward from mid-quotes at the strike nearest spot, and compared it to the listed future's mark:

**Conclusion on the triangle: not exploitable at retail size, and the reason is structural, not cyclical.** The three markets are on one venue, one margin engine, one index, with professional market makers arbitraging them continuously. What *is* usable is the inverse: the parity-implied forward is a free, accurate, per-expiry forward that you should use as the underlying in your IV calculations (as Deribit itself does), rather than the index. That materially changes your fitted skew.

## 4. SECTION 115BBH SAME-ASSET NETTING — **CONFIRMED: transaction-level. No netting.** And the section number he is using is obsolete.

**First: 115BBH no longer exists.** The Income-tax Act, 2025 replaced the 1961 Act. The successor is **Section 194, Table Sl. No. 4**, expressly mapped in the marginal note *"[Ss. 115B, 115BB, 115BBF, 115BBG, 115BBH and 115BBJ of the 1961 Act]"*. I read this in the Income-tax Act, 2025 as amended by Finance Act 2026. Any filing or memo he writes should cite s.194 Table Sl. No. 4, not 115BBH.

**The operative text**, verbatim, Sl. No. 4 (any person; income from transfer of any VDA; 30%), conditions:

> (a) No deduction in respect of any expenditure (other than cost of acquisition, if any) or allowance or **set off of any loss shall be allowed** to the assessee under any provision of this Act **in computing the income referred to in column C**; and
> (b) no set off of loss from transfer of the virtual digital asset computed herein shall be allowed against income computed under **any provision** of this Act to the assessee and such loss shall not be allowed to be carried forward to succeeding tax years.

Two independent bars. Condition (a) forbids set-off *in computing the VDA income itself* — that is what kills same-asset netting. Condition (b) then forbids set-off against anything else. Note (b) says "any provision", not "any **other** provision"; the narrowing word is absent, which is exactly what closes the inter-VDA route.

**Three converging confirmations:**

1. **Ministerial statement.** Pankaj Chaudhary, MoS Finance, answering Karti P. Chidambaram in the Lok Sabha on 21 March 2022: *"loss from the transfer of Virtual Digital Assets (VDA) will not be allowed to be set off against the income arising from transfer of another VDA."* This is the government's own reading, given in Parliament, and it addresses the same-asset question **directly**. *(Caveat: sansad.in returned HTTP 500 on every URL pattern I tried for AU2800; this quotation is from search-result text of that answer, not from the PDF. 2. **The enforcement mechanism, which is the strongest evidence and which I did open.** CBDT e-Filing **ITR-2 Validation Rules, AY 2025-26, v1.0** — https://www.incometax.gov.in/iec/foportal/sites/default/files/2025-07/CBDT__e-Filing_ITR%202_Validation%20Rules_AY%202025-26_V1.0.pdf — Rule 201 and Rule 202:

   > 202. In Schedule VDA, value at **'Total (Sum of all Positive Incomes of Capital Gain in Col. 7)'** should be equal to sum of col. 7 if head of income is selected as Capital Gain in col. 4

   The total field on the notified form is *literally labelled* "sum of all **positive** incomes". 3. **Statutory text**, above.

## 5. DEALER POSITIONING FROM OPEN INTEREST — **REFUTED as stated, but the failure opens a better door.** This is the most useful finding in the set after item 7.

Round one asserted dealer-positioning proxies are computable from OI plus a Black-Scholes gamma map. **The stated method is unidentified, and on NIFTY its standard sign convention is contradicted by NSE's own published data.**

### The identifying assumption, made explicit

The SqueezeMetrics GEX construction (white paper, March 2016, rev. 2017) computes per strike `Spot² × Γ × OI`, **call OI positive, put OI negative**. That sign convention is not a fact about the market; it is an assumption that **dealers are long every call and short every put** — equivalently, that customers sell all calls and buy all puts. OI is unsigned: every contract has a long and a short, and the exchange publishes only the total. **Nothing in an OI file distinguishes a dealer's long from a customer's long.** The convention requires, to be true:

1. Every option has a delta-hedging intermediary on one side;
2. Retail/institutional customer flow is systematically *long puts* (protection buying) and *short calls* (covered-call and overwriting programmes);
3. Net inventory is well approximated by cumulative OI rather than by signed flow.

In US index options, (2) is a defensible stylised fact grounded in the protection-buying bid. **It is the assumption that carries all the weight, and it is empirical, not structural.** Studies that actually identify dealer sign — Ni, Pearson, Poteshman and White on option trading's impact on underlying prices; Baltussen et al. on hedging demand and intraday momentum — use **signed order-flow data** (CBOE/ISE Open-Close, which flags buy-to-open vs sell-to-open), not open interest. That is the honest state of the art: sign comes from flow data, not OI.

## 7. THE RESIDUAL CONTRADICTION — **Both agents are partly right. Both stated the wrong mechanism. I settled it on real NIFTY data.**

This is the question that decides whether his SVI codebase contains a trade. I ran the adjudication rather than arguing it, using the NSE F&O bhavcopy for **27 August 2026** (NIFTY spot 24,090.85), 1,590 NIFTY option lines across 18 expiries.

### Agent B's "artefact" claim is CONFIRMED — but not for the reason given

Agent B blamed tick quantization, zero bids, and settlement prices from a fitted surface. **The settlement-price mechanism is real and large. The tick-quantization mechanism is quantitatively wrong in the range that matters.**

**Finding 1 — half the chain does not trade.** 821 of 1,590 NIFTY option lines (**51.6%**) had **zero volume** on the day. Per near expiry: 26–28% zero-volume even in the front three expiries.

**Finding 2 — untraded settlement prices are model output, and it is visible in the last digit.** NSE option ticks are Rs 0.05, so any genuine trade price lies on the 5-paise grid. Testing that grid:

| | n | settlement on the Rs 0.05 grid | ClsPric ≠ SttlmPric |
|---|---|---|---|
| Traded (vol > 0) | 769 | **90.5%** | 12% |
| Untraded (vol = 0) | 821 | **20.6%** | **100%** |

**79.4% of untraded settlement prices are off the tick grid entirely** — they cannot be observed prices. Examples: `NIFTY2691523550PE` close 133.00, settle **125.87**, vol 0. `NIFTY2690125900PE` close 1500.00, settle **1787.67**, vol 0. NSE Clearing confirms the method in principle: Black-Scholes with an assumed volatility is used to price contracts not traded, and the base price of newly introduced option contracts is "the theoretical value … based on the Black-Scholes model."

**Finding 3 — the imputation signature, which is the decisive exhibit.** On the 29 Sep 2026 expiry (T = 33d), four consecutive call strikes with **zero volume**:

| Strike | Volume | Settle | Implied vol |
|---|---|---|---|
| 25600 | 4,703 | 11.95 | **11.22%** |
| 25850 | **0** | 52.48 | 17.30% |
| 26100 | **0** | 34.02 | 17.21% |
| 26350 | **0** | 21.49 | 17.13% |
| 26600 | 162 | 3.55 | **14.11%** |
| 26850 | **0** | 7.93 | 17.00% |

The zero-volume strikes return **17.30, 17.21, 17.13, 17.00** — a near-constant, monotone, near-flat vol sequence — sitting **5–6 vol points above** their traded neighbours at 25600 and 26600. That is not a smile. **That is a flat-vol model writing its own answer into the data**, and it is exactly the failure agent B described. Fit SVI to a chain containing those rows and you will fit NSE's constant-volatility assumption in the wings and then discover a "residual" that is your own model disagreeing with theirs.

### Agent A's "residual is the surviving signal" claim is REFUTED as stated, but the tick objection against it fails

I computed, for every OTM strike, the IV uncertainty implied by **half a tick** (Rs 0.025) via `ΔIV = 0.025 / vega`:

**5-day expiry (1 Sep 2026), across the whole wing |k| ≤ 0.12:** half-tick IV uncertainty runs **0.00 to 0.17 vol points**. At k = −0.091 (22000 PE, settle 0.80, volume 64,558) it is **0.09** vol points against an IV of 28.66%. At k = +0.121 (27200 CE, settle 0.45, volume 22,247) it is **0.17** vol points against an IV of 34.96%.

Across that same wing the IV ranges from **6.4% to 33%**. **A half-tick is under 0.5% of the structure being measured.** Tick quantization is *not* what makes wing IVs unreliable in the liquid range. Agent B's stated mechanism is wrong on the numbers; the right mechanism is imputation and absent volume. Also note: **zero contracts settled at or below Rs 0.05** on the front expiry — the "zero bid" concern does not bind at EOD either.

But agent A is still refuted, for a different reason: **a residual measured against a surface fitted to a chain that is half imputed is not a market signal.** The signal and the contaminant are not separable at EOD.

### The adjudication, and the protocol that makes it testable

**His SVI codebase is infrastructure, not a trade — as currently fed.** It becomes a candidate trade only under filters that neither agent specified. Concretely:

**Quote-quality filters (all mandatory, all falsifiable):**
1. **Drop every strike with zero traded volume in the bar.** This alone removes ~52% of the EOD chain and all of the imputation signature.
2. **Never fit to `SttlmPric` or `ClsPric`.** Both are contaminated for untraded strikes; `ClsPric` is additionally stale. Fit to **intraday two-sided quotes** — which is precisely what his incoming minute-wise data provides and what the EOD bhavcopy structurally cannot.
3. **Require a two-sided quote with bid > 0** and a relative spread below a pre-registered threshold — set it from the data, not from taste.
4. **Screen on the tick grid as a cheap integrity check:** any "price" off the 5-paise grid in an intraday feed is imputed or erroneous. This is a free, decisive filter and it should run permanently.

**Moneyness and maturity range:**
5. **|log-moneyness| ≤ ~0.10 on the front weekly**, widened only where measured volume supports it. Beyond that, volume collapses (27200 CE: 22,247 contracts; 26600 CE: 1,645) and quote-driven IV noise grows non-linearly.
6. **Maturity: the front one or two expiries only.** Per SEBI FY26, 97% of index-option turnover is within 7 days of expiry and **1% beyond ten days**. There is no NIFTY term structure to trade. Any calendar or term-structure residual strategy is untradeable on this venue — that is a hard finding, and it kills a whole class of ideas cheaply.

**Error-bar construction — the part that decides everything:**
7. The error bar must be **the quoted bid-ask mapped into vol space** (`ΔIV = half-spread / vega`), **not** the half-tick. My computation shows the half-tick is 0.00–0.17 vol points; the *quoted spread* in the wings will be one to two orders of magnitude larger, and it is the quantity that determines whether a residual is real and, separately, whether it is capturable. Compute both; report both.
8. **Add a vega-weighted fit-uncertainty term.** An SVI slice fitted to n quotes has parameter uncertainty; the residual at strike k must be compared against the *combined* quote uncertainty and fit uncertainty at k, not against quote uncertainty alone. Round one's framing of "residual versus error bar" omitted the second term entirely, which is how a fitted-surface artefact gets mistaken for signal.

**The falsification test — pre-register it before looking:**

> **The residual is signal if, and only if, the sign of today's residual at strike k predicts the sign of tomorrow's change in that strike's mid-IV, out of sample, after subtracting the round-trip half-spread at that strike, on strikes that passed filters 1–6.**

Three specific ways it dies, and he should check each:
- **It reverses.** The residual predicts *mean reversion of the fit*, not of the market — i.e. it forecasts its own next-period recalibration. Test by re-fitting with a different SVI parameterisation (raw vs SVI-JW) and checking the residual survives. If it is parameterisation-dependent, it is an artefact of his own model.
- **It is real but uncapturable.** The residual is smaller than the half-spread at every strike where it is statistically distinguishable from zero. **This is the modal outcome, and it is exactly what Vilkov's correction turned out to be** — the entire 0DTE result set inverted on a cost term two orders of magnitude smaller than a NIFTY wing spread. He should expect this and design to detect it early rather than discovering it after six months.
- **It is a liquidity proxy.** The residual is largest precisely where volume is lowest, meaning he has rediscovered the illiquidity premium. Test by regressing residual magnitude on contemporaneous volume and spread; if those two regressors absorb it, there is nothing left.

**What changes on the answer.** If the residual survives all three, his existing SVI/SSVI work is the core of a trade and everything else is plumbing. If it does not, the codebase is still worth having — as the surface that prices and risk-manages positions he takes for other reasons — but it is **not** the alpha, and he should stop treating it as such. **On the evidence available at EOD, I cannot resolve this, and neither could either round-one agent: the question is genuinely intraday-only.** His incoming minute-wise NIFTY data is the correct and possibly the only instrument. That is the good news — the decisive experiment is one he can actually run, in weeks, and the pre-registered falsification above is the whole specification.
